implementation_notes: The default modern realization: the contract is a Protocol class in its own module and implementations never inherit from it - the type checker verifies conformance structurally, which means an implementation that cannot be modified (third-party or legacy) still satisfies the contract. Use this whenever conformance should be checked statically without forcing an import edge from the implementation back to the contract module.
pitfalls: Protocols are erased at runtime: isinstance() needs @runtime_checkable, which then checks only method presence.
A structural match can be accidental - a class with a same-named method satisfies the Protocol without meaning to.
Without a type checker in CI the Protocol is documentation only; add mypy or pyright to the pipeline.

variants.name: Nominal contract with abc.ABC
variants.implementation_notes: The classic nominal realization: implementations inherit from the abstract base class (or are registered with ABCMeta.register), and instantiation of an incomplete subclass raises TypeError. Choose it when the contract must be enforced at runtime, when implementations share helper code, or when the set of implementations is a closed, enumerated family.
pitfalls: abc.ABC enforces at instantiation time only; subclasses that skip super().__init__() or register() as virtual subclasses bypass the check.
Inheritance creates an import edge from the implementation module to the contract module, which the Protocol form avoids.
ABCMeta adds metaclass constraints: mixing ABC with a custom metaclass requires care.
